analysis.one_liner: Strips health and malpractice insurers of their antitrust exemption so they can be sued for price fixing and market division.
analysis.headline: The House Judiciary Committee approved the bill 20-9 in fall 2009 and put it on the House calendar, but no chamber ever voted on it, and the health insurance industry kept its broad antitrust exemption when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Health insurers have long operated under a special carve-out in a 1945 law, the McCarran-Ferguson Act, that largely shields the insurance industry from federal antitrust laws. This bill would have said plainly that health insurers and medical malpractice insurers cannot legally fix prices, rig bids, or divide up markets. It cleared the House Judiciary Committee on a 20-9 vote in October 2009, but was never brought up for a vote by the full House or Senate.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who buy health insurance and employers who pay for it would benefit if the bill passed: health and malpractice insurers would face federal antitrust suits for price fixing, bid rigging, and dividing up markets, which could increase competition and put downward pressure on premiums. Small insurers and medical providers competing against coordinated giants would also gain a level playing field.

how_it_helps.text: It removes the industry's McCarran-Ferguson shield against federal antitrust law, so insurers could be sued for price fixing, bid rigging, or dividing up markets like any other business [S2][S3][S4].
It applies to both health insurance and medical malpractice insurance, where coordinated pricing among a small number of insurers was a particular concern [S1][S4].
It preserves state regulators' own authority to gather data and set rates, so state oversight continues [S4].

analysis.who_pays: Health and malpractice insurers would bear the cost: they would lose their exemption from federal antitrust law and face litigation and liability for coordinated conduct, plus the compliance burden of pricing without shared coordination. Some analysts argued insurers might pass added legal costs back into premiums.

drawbacks.text: The reported bill narrows the original proposal: it expressly allows insurers to keep sharing historical loss data, setting loss development factors, and performing actuarial services, so some coordinated pricing inputs survive the reform [S3][S4].

Critics of removing the industry's antitrust exemption argued that joint data-gathering and rate-setting helps insurers price risk accurately, and that exposing them to antitrust suits could raise premiums or reduce coverage in some markets — though the reported version's exclusions were designed to blunt exactly this objection [S3][S4].

The bill targets only price fixing, bid rigging, and market allocation; it does not directly cap premiums or address consolidation through mergers, so its practical effect on premiums may be limited [S1][S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — making health insurers compete under the same antitrust rules as nearly every other industry — is real but modest in magnitude: it addresses one contributor to rising premiums, not the whole problem. The main cost is administrative and legal: insurers would face antitrust litigation risk, and some shared data-gathering that arguably keeps premiums accurate is preserved by the exclusion in any case. On balance the bill's costs were small relative to its benefit to consumers; the more honest criticism is that it does too little too narrowly.

outcome.mechanism: The House Judiciary Committee approved the bill on a 20-9 vote and put it on the House calendar, but House leaders never brought it to the floor, the Senate never acted, and the bill died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced September 17, 2009, and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, which held a subcommittee hearing in October [S6].
On October 21, 2009, the committee voted 20-9 to order the bill reported with amendments [S6].
On November 2, 2009, the committee reported the amended bill (H. Rept. 111-322) and it was placed on the Union Calendar, the list of bills awaiting House floor action [S3][S6].
No floor vote ever occurred in the House and no action followed in the Senate; the bill died when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011 [S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers are the clear winners: their exemption from federal antitrust law survived, and they can continue coordinated pricing and market division free of antitrust suit. Consumers gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. John Conyers
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and, as committee chair, guided it through subcommittee hearing and full-committee markup to a 20-9 vote ordering it reported.

for.name: House Judiciary Committee majority
for.what_they_did: Voted 20-9 on October 21, 2009 to order the bill reported with amendments.

sides.party_line_note: The committee vote to advance the bill was 20-9; the Democratic-run committee advanced it with broad (though not unanimous) support, and all 19 cosponsors were Democrats [S5][S6].

industries.note: The bill strips health insurers of the McCarran-Ferguson exemption to federal antitrust law, exposing price fixing, bid rigging, and market allocation to lawsuits. Insurers' interest in keeping the exemption runs against consumers, who pay the premiums set under less competition.
Malpractice insurers, whose markets are small and concentrated, also lose the exemption for coordinated pricing. Their premiums ultimately feed into doctors' costs, which pass through to patients.

The bill expressly does not touch the information-gathering and rate-setting activities of state insurance commissions, so regulators keep their existing tools; some shared data collection by insurers is also preserved under the exclusions.
